name: Ivan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice on a transmission maintenance crew for Meridian Power, the big private electricity company. Transmission means the tall steel towers carrying high-voltage lines between towns, not the poles on your street. We drive out to the hills, check and replace insulators, tighten bolts, fix the earth wires, and these days a lot of it starts with drone pictures. I'm 58. Two years ago I was running the IT helpdesk for a hospital group, until they replaced most of us with an AI chatbot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and that the result is obvious: the line holds or it doesn't. What wears me out is heights, if I'm honest. Ninety metres up a tower, I'm the slowest climber on the crew by a distance, and Kofi, our crew lead, has to talk me through the transfer points. The funny part is I'm the one everyone asks when the drone software crashes, and I use AI every day to look up specs and draft my reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'll describe five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, half-joking, that it's a shame it didn't stay mostly hype two years earlier, because I'd still have my old job. Online I'd probably post a long thread about how much of the AI talk was sales. I'd be careful not to gloat, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my bet was right. I left a desk for a tower partly because I thought hands-on work would hold, and in this picture it does. I'd get my ticket and do eight good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as now. Finish the apprenticeship in 2027, keep using AI tools for the paperwork and specs, and maybe get my drone pilot licence because the crew needs more than one. Nothing changes at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a slightly bitter laugh at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I watched eleven people on my helpdesk lose their jobs to a chatbot that still can't reset a password properly. If it all turns out to be hype, then we lost those jobs to a fashion. That's worse, somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Anjali works as a pharmacist, we've got about four months saved after I burned through some of it between jobs, and the kids are grown. Dev's a software developer and Meera's a vet, so they're off our books.

S0.say: He'd half-joke that he wished AI had stayed hype two years earlier so he'd still have his helpdesk job. He'd post a long thread about the sales talk but try not to gloat.
S0.think: Privately it means his bet on hands-on work paid off. He'd get his qualification and have eight good years on the towers.
S0.do: Carries on: finishes the apprenticeship in 2027, keeps using AI tools for specs and reports, and considers getting a drone pilot licence because the crew needs a second pilot. Changes nothing at home.
S0.feel: Calm, with a slightly bitter laugh behind it.
S0.quote: If it all turns out to be hype, then we lost those jobs to a fashion. That's worse, somehow.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan has already lost one job to AI and still uses it every day without resentment towards the tool itself. The bitterness is aimed at decisions made in its name. He's the slowest climber on his crew but the go-to person for the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make line work safer, and that the unions should be shaping it from day one, not reacting. Fewer climbs, better fault-finding, drones doing the dangerous inspections. I'd write that on the union forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this one is good for me. I'm a poor climber and a good tech person. If the job shifts towards drones, sensors and data, I move from the bottom of the crew to somewhere useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the drone pilot licence this winter, about 1,500 out of my own pocket if the company won't pay. I'd volunteer for every pilot project Meridian runs, and I'd set up a little AI tool to sort our inspection photos, then show it to Kofi. Meanwhile I'd finish the apprenticeship, because you need to understand a tower to judge a picture of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit excited, which surprises me after what happened last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, oddly. He's the best climber I've ever seen and he hates screens. If the value moves from the tower to the tablet, people like him lose standing they've earned over twenty years. I'd want the union to make sure the old skills still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost a job to AI, and now you'd volunteer for every AI project. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The helpdesk didn't lose to AI, it lost to managers who used AI to cut costs and kept the savings. The tool's neutral. I'd rather be the one holding it than the one it's pointed at.

S1.say: He'd say the change could make line work safer, with drones doing dangerous inspections, and that unions must shape it from the start. He'd post that on the union forum.
S1.think: Privately he thinks this picture helps him: he's a poor climber but strong with technology, so a shift towards drones, sensors and data lifts him from the bottom of the crew.
S1.do: Books a drone pilot licence this winter, paying about 1,500 himself if needed, and volunteers for every company pilot project. Builds a small AI tool to sort inspection photos and keeps finishing the apprenticeship.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, which surprises him.
S1.quote: The tool's neutral. I'd rather be the one holding it than the one it's pointed at.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan is the rare person whose junior standing could rise in this picture, because his weakness is climbing and his strength is technology. He blames managers, not tools, for his helpdesk job loss. He worries for the crew lead whose hard-won skills might lose value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an automation tax and a basic income now, not in five years, and that every company replacing people with machines should pay into it. I'd be organising, writing to politicians, posting everything. I'd say I warned people in 2024.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I've lived the first act of this already. I know what it's like at 56 to send out forty applications and hear nothing. At 60, with robots climbing towers too, there's no next move like the one I made. And Anjali's pharmacy is the kind of job that goes early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut to what we need and push savings from four months towards eight. I'd try to get onto whatever team installs and maintains the robots at Meridian, because someone has to unload them, fix them and sign them off for a while. I'd also join the union's campaign for an automation tax and give it my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've been here before and I got up again, but I know exactly how bad the bottom feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you got up again last time. What did that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight months, most of our savings, and Anjali carrying us. And the honest truth is that it took this job existing, a job that wanted a 56-year-old beginner. In two-year AGI that job doesn't exist, and that's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev, your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev already worries more than I do, because coders are first in line. I'd tell him to save like mad and not to be ashamed if he has to move back in for a while. We've got the spare room, and I'd rather have him there than drowning in rent.

S2.say: He'd call for an automation tax and a basic income immediately, paid by companies that replace people with machines. He'd organise, write to politicians and remind people he warned them in 2024.
S2.think: Privately he knows how bad job hunting at 56 was, and at 60 with robots on towers there'd be no equivalent escape. He also expects his wife's pharmacy job to go early.
S2.do: Cuts spending to essentials and pushes savings from four months towards eight. Tries to join the team that installs and maintains the robots at his company, and gives his evenings to the union's automation tax campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because he's recovered before and knows how bad the bottom feels.
S2.quote: And the honest truth is that it took this job existing, a job that wanted a 56-year-old beginner.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan's past job loss works both ways: he knows he can recover, but he also knows his recovery depended on a job that two-year AGI would erase. He'd move towards the robots rather than away from them. He offers his son the spare room without hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but with a plan attached: five years is enough to build the training and the safety net if we start in 2027. I'd push the union to demand that lineworkers get first claim on the robot technician jobs. Online I'd be the annoying guy posting timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to make the jump properly. I'd be 63, I'd have my ticket, my drone licence and a robotics course behind me. I might end up as one of the people who sends the robots up the towers and checks their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the drone licence. Years two and three, a part-time robotics maintenance certificate at the technical college, evenings, and I'd ask Meridian to fund half. I'd save the extra I make once qualified, and I'd help Anjali look at moving from the pharmacy counter into a clinical role, which might last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than anxious. It feels like a hard climb I've got time to rig for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point in those five years when you'd know it was really coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the first robot does a full insulator swap on a live tower without a person on the structure. I'd give it a year after that. That's my signal to stop hedging and put everything into the robot side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep talking about yourself moving up. Who gets left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, again, and the older lads who never learned the screens. I'd want the union to fight for proper buyouts for them, paid early retirement. Not everyone should have to become me, and not everyone wants to.

S3.say: He'd argue that five years is enough to build training and a safety net if work starts in 2027, and push for lineworkers to get first claim on robot technician jobs. Online he'd keep posting timelines.
S3.think: Privately he believes five years lets him make the jump properly: at 63, with his qualification, a drone licence and a robotics course, he could be one of those who sends robots up towers and checks their work.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence in year one, then studies a part-time robotics maintenance certificate in years two and three, asking his employer to fund half. Saves the pay rise from qualifying and helps his wife look at a longer-lasting clinical role.
S3.feel: Uneasy rather than anxious, like a hard climb he has time to rig for.
S3.quote: When the first robot does a full insulator swap on a live tower without a person on the structure.
S3.fieldNote: Ivan has a precise trigger for when he'd go all in, which is typical of his engineering mindset. The extra three years turn defence into a training plan. He's aware that his path doesn't suit everyone and argues for buyouts for older colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it the politicians should answer for it. I'd keep pushing for an automation tax and a shorter working week. I'd also be telling people, kindly, to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd retire around 66 in 2034, probably after a few years in a robot maintenance role. The real stakes are Dev's and Meera's careers, and I'd want them to use the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify, get the drone licence, and do the robotics certificate over three or four years instead of cramming it. Help the union set up a training scheme so older lineworkers can move across. And I'd keep using AI every day, because the people who know these tools will run the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe even curious about what the job looks like at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you picture your last day at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like it to be at a control desk with a robot crew on a tower in the hills, and Kofi beside me telling me I'm doing it wrong. That would feel like the right ending to a strange career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust ten years to be enough. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I trusted the hospital to look after its staff and it didn't. So I'm calm about my own plan, and not at all calm about whether governments will use the time. That part I can only vote and campaign on.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift and say politicians should answer for wasting it, while pushing for an automation tax and a shorter working week. He'd kindly tell people to start learning now.
S4.think: Privately he feels comfortable: he'd retire around 66 in 2034, probably after a few years in robot maintenance. The bigger stakes are his children's careers.
S4.do: Keeps going, qualifies, gets the drone licence and takes the robotics certificate over three or four years. Helps the union set up a training scheme for older lineworkers and keeps using AI tools every day.
S4.feel: Calm and a little curious about how the job will look at the end.
S4.quote: I'd like it to be at a control desk with a robot crew on a tower in the hills, and Kofi beside me telling me I'm doing it wrong.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ivan is calm about his own path and openly unsure about whether governments will act. His trust in institutions was damaged by the hospital layoffs. He sees his tech habits as his ticket to staying relevant into retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I know how a sudden job loss feels in your fifties, and that picture takes away the escape route I used. What would help is money while you adjust, an automation tax funding a basic income, and real access to the new technician jobs for people already in the trade. Don't make 60-year-olds compete with 20-year-olds for the only courses going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people whether they trust their employer to share the gains. That's the real question, not whether the technology works. I spent eighteen years keeping a hospital's computers running, and I was let go with a leaving card and a chatbot doing my job by Friday.

headlineQuote: I spent eighteen years keeping a hospital's computers running, and I was let go with a leaving card and a chatbot doing my job by Friday.
portrait: Ivan Gupta is a 58-year-old apprentice on a transmission tower crew for Meridian Power, a large private electricity company, who moved into line work after an AI chatbot replaced his hospital IT helpdesk team. He's progressive and union-minded but uses AI every day and blames managers, not tools, for his past job loss. He's the slowest climber on the crew but the person everyone calls when the drone software crashes. In the milder pictures he sees a chance to rise through drone and sensor work. AGI in two years makes him anxious because it removes the kind of escape route he used before, while five or ten years give him time to retrain into robot maintenance.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because it would remove the escape route he used after losing his helpdesk job, at an age when job hunting is already hard.
whatWouldHelp: Income support while people adjust, an automation tax funding a basic income, and real access to new technician jobs for workers already in the trade.
